memory.title: Memory map
memory.attachFirst: Attach a process to show its memory map.

search.title: What do you want to find?

scan.nextScanHint: Change the value in the game, pick what happened from the list, then click Next Scan.

modules.intro: Optional KillEngine dependencies: installed/missing status and in-UI installation (local scripts, network download, UAC prompt). Install missing modules before exporting the package to another machine.
modules.empty: No module detected — run a scan.

edr.confirmDesc: Test if the EDR blocks code injection on the attached process. This simulates VirtualAllocEx + WriteProcessMemory + CreateRemoteThread.
edr.addExclusionDesc: Add the build/bin folder to Microsoft Defender exclusions. This requires UAC elevation.
edr.step1Desc: Adds the build folder to Defender exclusions. Run in an elevated PowerShell.
edr.step2Desc: Completely disables Windows Defender via registry. Requires a reboot.
edr.step3Desc: Disables only behavior monitoring (less aggressive than step 2).
edr.confirmDisableDesc: Completely disables Windows Defender via the registry (UAC elevation required). Reduces your system's protection — remember to re-enable it once testing is done. ⚠ A restart is required for the change to take effect.
edr.confirmReenableDesc: Removes the registry override disabling Windows Defender (UAC elevation required). ⚠ A restart is required for protection to actually be restored — Defender stays disabled until then despite the key being removed.
edr.confirmDisableBehaviorDesc: Disables only Windows Defender's behavior monitoring via the registry (UAC elevation required) — less aggressive than a full disable. ⚠ A restart is required for the change to take effect.
edr.confirmReenableBehaviorDesc: Removes the registry override disabling behavior monitoring (UAC elevation required). ⚠ A restart is required for protection to actually be restored.
edr.manualWarning: ⚠ These changes reduce your system's protection. Re-enable them after your test sessions.

debugPriv.confirmDesc: Enable the SeDebugName privilege for the current process — required for hardware breakpoints and injection.

stealth.confirmDesc: Apply the SC2 stealth profile (PEB anti-debug + process mask + dll mask) to the attached process. This makes KillEngine more discreet.

error.notAttached: Attach a process before connecting to its WebView2 target.
error.connectFailed: Failed to connect to the WebView2 target.
error.disconnectFailed: Failed to disconnect the WebView2 inspector.

risk.connectMessage: Opens a CDP (Chrome DevTools Protocol) connection to an external process to read its JavaScript/DOM state. Read-only by default, but any later JS evaluation can also modify that state.
risk.evaluateMessage: Runs the given JavaScript code in the connected page — can read or modify the target's state depending on the code executed.

warning.notAttached: Attach a process to list its WebView2 CDP targets (see the Process view).

probe.title: JS context reconnaissance
probe.hint: Lists variables/functions added by the page (as opposed to native Chromium noise), so you know what to evaluate without guessing blindly.

adresse.definition: A precise location in a process's memory, written in hexadecimal (e.g. 0x7FF6FB1300E4). That's where a value lives at a given moment — it can change every time the program restarts.

aob.definition: A distinctive sequence of bytes found in the program's code, used as a stable landmark to relocate a specific spot even after a restart — unlike a raw memory address, which changes every launch.

aslr.definition: A Windows security mechanism that randomly relocates a program's modules in memory on every launch. That's why an absolute address found yesterday no longer works today, and why AOB signatures or pointer chains are used instead.

breakpoint.definition: A deliberate pause in the program's execution at a specific point in the code, used to observe or intercept a memory write at the exact moment it happens.

clr.definition: The .NET (C#) runtime engine. KillEngine's CLR Inspector walks the program's live objects (the "managed heap") directly instead of guessing addresses, which is more reliable for games/apps written in C#.

dll.definition: A shared code library file that Windows loads into a program. Injection means making an extra DLL (e.g. the CLR helper) load inside the target process.

edr.definition: Security software (e.g. Microsoft Defender for Endpoint) that monitors and can block actions considered suspicious, such as writing into another program's executable code. Some AOB patches can be rejected because of an EDR, independent of any KillEngine bug.

freeze.definition: Repeatedly rewriting a value (or intercepting every write attempt) to keep it from changing even if the program tries to modify it — for example to keep health or ammo constant.

heap.definition: The memory area where a program dynamically creates its objects while running (as opposed to code or fixed data). An address in the heap often changes when the object is recreated (new game, scene change), which is why pointer chains are useful.

hex.definition: A way of writing numbers in base 16 (digits 0-9 then A-F), used for every memory address. An address like 0x1A4 is not a game value, it's a location.

hooking.definition: Redirecting an existing function in the program so it first runs through code added by KillEngine (e.g. to count calls or change behavior), then resumes normally — unlike a patch, the original function isn't replaced, just intercepted along the way.

injection.definition: Making code (usually a DLL) load inside another already-running process, in order to inspect or influence it from within.

kernel.definition: The core of the operating system, with higher privileges than normal programs. KillEngine can use a kernel driver for operations Windows normally refuses to a regular program.

locator.definition: The method a Trainer feature uses to relocate an address: absolute (the raw address, doesn't survive a restart), AOB (code signature, survives), or pointer chain (module + offsets path, survives and handles heap objects).

lua.definition: A simple scripting language used in the Lua tab to automate actions in KillEngine (via ke.call(...)) without recompiling the program — useful for repeating a sequence of actions or writing a small custom tool.

module.definition: An executable file or DLL loaded in memory by a process. A "module + offset" address (e.g. SC2.exe+0x4A1B2) stays stable across launches, unlike an absolute address.

offset.definition: A fixed distance, in bytes, between a stable landmark (a module, or an object field) and the actual target. Used in pointer chains and "module + offset" addresses.

pageguard.definition: A technique that traps a memory page to get notified as soon as a program tries to read or write it, without going through a classic breakpoint.

pipe.definition: A communication channel between two programs on the same machine. KillEngine exposes an automation pipe that lets an external script (PowerShell, Lua) drive the application without going through UI clicks.

pointerchain.definition: A pointer is an address that itself contains another address. A pointer chain starts from a stable module and walks several successive offsets to relocate a heap object, even after it was recreated at a different address.

processus.definition: A running instance of a program on Windows (e.g. Solitaire.exe). KillEngine must be "attached" to a process before it can read or modify its memory.

riskgate.definition: KillEngine's confirmation guard rail: before any action that actually changes something (write, patch, freeze...), a dialog asks for explicit confirmation.

correlation.definition: A statistical measure (Pearson coefficient, between -1 and 1) showing whether two watched addresses move together — useful for spotting that a "displayed" field just mirrors a "source" field, or that two values are linked by the same game mechanism. 1 = move exactly together, 0 = no apparent link.

stealth.definition: A set of modules that hide KillEngine's attachment from a target's anti-debug/anti-cheat mechanisms: antiDebug (hides the debugger from the program's own checks), processMask (renames the KillEngine process), dllMask (hides DLLs injected by KillEngine). Toggle by profile in Settings, or after a detectability analysis that recommends what to activate based on what was found in the target.

scan.definition: A search across the whole process memory to find addresses holding a given value (exact scan) or varying in a certain way (increased, decreased, unknown value). This is the basis of every value search in KillEngine.

signature.definition: See AOB — a byte pattern used to reliably relocate a specific spot in the code, instead of a raw address.

speedhack.definition: A feature that artificially speeds up or slows down how a program perceives time passing, without touching its memory (e.g. to speed up a loading screen or slow down a too-fast enemy).

stack.definition: A temporary memory area a program uses for its current function calls. Different from the heap, which holds dynamically created objects.

thread.definition: An independent execution line inside the same process. A program can have several threads active at once, which matters for techniques like breakpoints or freezing.

trainer.definition: The tab that turns a found address or action into a reusable feature (freeze, write) that can be toggled with one click or a keyboard shortcut, without redoing a whole search.

typevaleur.definition: The format a value is stored in memory as: whole number (Int32, Int64...), decimal number (Float32/Float64), text (String), or raw byte sequence (Array of Bytes). Picking the right type matters for a scan or write to work.

uwp.definition: Universal Windows Platform — a type of Windows app (often installed via the Microsoft Store) with its own storage rules (LocalSettings, sandboxed folders) different from a classic program.

webview2.definition: The web engine (Chromium/Edge) some Windows apps embed for their UI — often Store apps. KillEngine's WebView2 Inspector queries its JavaScript state via the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) instead of raw memory, useful when a classic memory scan only finds engine noise (V8/Blink) instead of real data.

writeprocessmemory.definition: The low-level Windows function that writes bytes into another process's memory. This is the final mechanism behind most of KillEngine's writes and patches.

xor.definition: A simple logical operation sometimes used by programs to slightly mask a value in memory (e.g. storing value XOR key instead of the raw value) to throw off a direct scan. A value "XOR-obfuscated" won't be found by a plain exact scan on the displayed number.

findWhatAccesses.title: Find what accesses
findWhatAccesses.intro: Captures the program instructions that READ this address (read-only, no write).
findWhatAccesses.empty: No access captured during the observation window.

network.title: Network
network.intro: Analyze and control network traffic of the attached process.

proxy.title: HTTP Proxy
proxy.intro: Intercepts and modifies HTTP/HTTPS requests from the game in real time.

dnsSpoof.title: DNS Spoof
dnsSpoof.intro: Redirects a domain to a local IP via the Windows hosts file.

lagSwitch.title: Lag switch
lagSwitch.intro: Artificially delays the game's network responses.

block.title: Network block
block.intro: Blocks all inbound/outbound traffic of the attached process via a Windows Firewall rule.

read.label: Read only
read.detail: These tools read the target process memory without ever modifying it.

write.label: Writes memory
write.detail: These tools modify the target process data. Reversible through Rollback, but a wrong address can crash it.

code.label: Modifies code
code.detail: These tools attach a debugger or rewrite the target process instructions. Crash and detection risk. Keep it to software you control.

find.title: 1. Find
find.what: Narrow the whole process memory down to a handful of candidate addresses.

inspect.title: 2. Inspect
inspect.what: Work out which candidate is the real value, and which stable path leads to it.

act.title: 3. Act
act.what: Write or freeze the value. From here on the target process is modified.

persist.title: 4. Persist
persist.what: Turn what works into a code signature, then a patch, then a reusable Trainer feature.

processKernelAccess.title: Memory access mode
processKernelAccess.what: Chooses the interactive memory read/write path after attaching: Standard uses the usual usermode APIs; Kernel routes memory previews, the hex viewer, and simple writes through KillEngineKernel when the driver is ready.
processKernelAccess.when: You do not need kernel access to open a process, list modules, or run the first full scans. Choose Kernel when you want to work in ring 0 on the addresses you found, or when a standard write fails or does not stick.
processKernelAccess.cost: The driver must already be loaded and report memory access. Full scans still use the standard reader until the scan engine gets a complete reader abstraction; Kernel mode applies to interactive, verifiable reads/writes.
processKernelAccess.example: Solitaire: attach the process in Kernel mode, scan 175 then 185, then read both candidates and write 1337 to the right address. If a value reverts even through kernel, find the source with Find what writes.

regionContext.title: Active region
regionContext.what: Details the memory region of the selected address: bounds, protection, state and type.
regionContext.when: To understand why a write fails, or to check whether the address sits in Private data rather than Mapped or Image memory.
regionContext.example: A candidate address sits at 0x1A2B..., type Private, RW protection. That is real program data (not a read-only mapped file) — a good sign for writing to it without an access error.

scanExact.title: Exact scan
scanExact.what: Finds every memory address holding exactly the value you typed.
scanExact.when: When the value is visible on screen and stays stable. Fastest starting point.
scanExact.cost: Read only. The first scan can return thousands of results: that is expected, Next Scan narrows them down.
scanExact.example: You see 41250 as gold on screen. Type 41250, pick Int32, click Scan. Hundreds of addresses come back — that is expected, it is the starting point, not the final answer.

nextScan.title: Next scan
nextScan.what: Re-reads only the existing candidates and keeps those matching the chosen comparison.
nextScan.when: After a first scan, as soon as the value changed in the program. Repeat until only a few addresses remain.
nextScan.cost: Read only. Unchanged is the noisiest comparison: it keeps almost everything.
nextScan.example: After scanning for 41250, you spend 500 in-game (new displayed gold: 40750). Type 40750, click Next Scan Exact: the list drops to a few dozen addresses.

unknown.title: Unknown initial value
unknown.what: Snapshots memory without knowing the value, then compares successive snapshots through it went up, it went down, it changed, it is stable.
unknown.when: When the value is not displayed as a number: health bar, gauge, percentage, or encrypted value.
unknown.cost: Read only, but the snapshot uses temporary disk space. Expect 3 to 5 comparisons before the list is usable.
unknown.example: The health bar shows no exact number. Click Capture, take a hit in-game, then click it went down. Repeat 2-3 times until only 1-5 candidates remain.

uiString.title: UI string trace
uiString.what: Starts from the text shown on screen rather than the number, then walks back to the numeric source or pointer feeding it.
uiString.when: When numeric scans find nothing: modern engines, decoupled UI, value recomputed at display time.
uiString.cost: Read only. Many matches are display copies rather than the real source: use Auto origin to tell them apart.
uiString.example: A plain Int32 scan finds nothing for the on-screen "45". Run Scan text on "45": it surfaces every memory location holding that text, then Analyze sources looks for the number feeding it right next to it.

candidates.title: Candidates
candidates.what: Paginated list of addresses kept by the current scan, with their re-read value and a confidence score.
candidates.when: Throughout: this is the working set. Select addresses to write, watch, or send to the Assistant.
candidates.cost: Read only. Re-reading queries the target process on every refresh.
candidates.example: 3 addresses remain after narrowing. Check them, then click Send to Assistant to keep the conversation going with these active leads without retyping addresses.

write.title: Write / Freeze
write.what: Writes a value to the selected addresses, and can rewrite it in a loop (freeze) so it does not drop back.
write.when: Once only a few candidates remain. Test in small batches before freezing.
write.cost: Modifies the target process memory. A wrong address can crash it. Every write stays reversible through Rollback.
write.example: 2 candidates remain after narrowing. Type 999999 as the value, click Write: KillEngine computes and shows the Write plan before the final click that actually changes memory.

freezeBp.title: Breakpoint freeze
freezeBp.what: Sets a hardware breakpoint on the address and rewrites the value at the exact moment the program tries to change it.
freezeBp.when: When polling freeze flickers because the target rewrites the value faster than the polling interval.
freezeBp.cost: Attaches the Windows debugger to the process. Can be detected or disturb the target.
freezeBp.example: Regular freeze at 16 ms flickers because the game rewrites the value faster than one tick. Switch to Freeze BP: the value is corrected the instant the game tries to write it.

watchLive.title: Live watch
watchLive.what: Watches up to 200 addresses and shows their values in real time, without clicking address by address.
watchLive.when: To tell candidates apart: the right address follows what you do in the program.
watchLive.cost: Read only. A large watch batch increases read load.
watchLive.example: You have 4 suspect candidates. Click Watch on each, then play: the one that moves exactly as expected (drops by 10 after a hit, say) is the right one.

findWhatWrites.title: Find what writes
findWhatWrites.what: Attaches the debugger and captures the instruction writing to this address: its RIP, module and disassembly.
findWhatWrites.when: To go from knowing the address to knowing the code that computes it, and turn that into a stable patch.
findWhatWrites.cost: Attaches the Windows debugger. Change the value in the program during the capture window, otherwise nothing is caught.
findWhatWrites.example: The address you found refuses to stay frozen. Click Find what writes, then land a hit in-game during the capture window: KillEngine shows the exact instruction writing that value, with its module and offset.

autoDissect.title: Auto-dissect
autoDissect.intro: Automatically scans memory to find all instances of a saved structure template.
autoDissect.empty: No instance found matching the template.
autoDissect.what: Walks all writable regions of the process and matches template fields to automatically discover all entities (players, units, items) of the same type.
autoDissect.when: When you've saved a structure template (e.g. a player layout) and want to find ALL instances of that structure in memory at once.
autoDissect.cost: Memory read only, no write. Can be slow on large processes (scans all writable regions).
autoDissect.example: You found a player layout (HP@+0x0, Mana@+0x4, XP@+0x8). Click Auto-dissect: KillEngine scans all memory and returns addresses of ALL players/units with that same layout.

findWhatAccesses.title: Find what accesses
findWhatAccesses.intro: Captures the program instructions that READ this address (read-only, no write).
findWhatAccesses.empty: No access captured during the observation window.
findWhatAccesses.what: Attaches the debugger and captures instructions that read this address — useful to trace computation sources without modifying memory.
findWhatAccesses.when: When you want to know WHO reads a value without modifying it (e.g. understanding where a calculation comes from before deciding what to write).
findWhatAccesses.cost: Attaches the Windows debugger. Change the value in the program during the capture window.
findWhatAccesses.example: You found a value's address but don't know how it's computed. Click Find what accesses, then trigger the action in-game: KillEngine shows all instructions reading this address.

disassembleBackward.title: Disassemble backward
disassembleBackward.what: Reads the bytes right before the instruction captured by Find what writes, and reconstructs the instructions that lead up to it (read-only, no debugger attach). Instructions with a simple [register+displacement] memory operand are highlighted as "candidate fields".
disassembleBackward.when: When a write never sticks (the value drifts back on its own): the targeted field is often the displayed result of an animated counter (e.g. displayed = current + (target - current) × progress), recomputed every frame and therefore impossible to hold with a direct write. The real source fields (current/target) are almost always read just before, in the few instructions preceding the write.
disassembleBackward.cost: Memory read only, no debugger attach, no write. Requires a RIP already captured via Find what writes.
disassembleBackward.example: Real case: a card game's XP never held after a direct write. Find what writes captured `mov [rsi+0x900], edx` (the displayed field). Disassemble backward traced it back to `mov ecx, [rsi+0x904]` (current) and `mov eax, [rsi+0x908]` (target) right before a float interpolation. Writing to `[rsi+0x908]` (the target) fixed it — never to `[rsi+0x900]`.

testCandidateFields.title: Test automatically
testCandidateFields.what: Writes a transient test value to each candidate field found by Disassemble backward (resolved internally, no need to have run it first), waits a few seconds, reads back, then always restores the original value. Classifies each field as "holds" or "reverts".
testCandidateFields.when: Replaces reading raw assembly by hand: instead of guessing which of the listed [register+displacement] fields is the real "current"/"target" of an animated counter, let KillEngine prove it empirically. The field that "holds" is almost always the right one to write.
testCandidateFields.cost: Actually writes to memory, even if transient and restored afterward — treated as a normal write (confirmation required). Up to 5 fields tested, ~12 seconds max each.
testCandidateFields.example: Real case: on a card game's XP, the test showed [rsi+0x900] (displayed) and [rsi+0x904] (current) reverting on their own within seconds, but [rsi+0x908] (target) holding — confirming the right address to write without reading a single line of assembly.

aob.title: AOB signatures
aob.what: Searches a byte signature inside the program code, then offers to patch the matched instruction.
aob.when: To build a feature that survives a restart: an address changes every session, a code signature does not.
aob.cost: Modifies the executable code. A signature matching several places is blocked, because patching the wrong one crashes the target.
aob.example: Find what writes located the instruction at SC2.exe+0x4A1B2. Click Signature to generate a stable AOB, then Analyze to see the suggested patches (NOP the write, force a value, etc.) ranked by risk.

writeAtomic.title: Atomic multi-address write
writeAtomic.what: Writes several addresses at the same time, briefly suspending every thread of the target process during the operation, instead of writing one address after another. Useful when a target keeps several redundant copies of the same value and silently corrects the one that no longer matches the others.
writeAtomic.when: A normal write on one address succeeded (verified in memory) but nothing changes on screen, and repeated next scans show that 2 to 5 addresses stay identical to each other every cycle: that's the sign of redundant copies. Select those addresses and write them together instead of one at a time.
writeAtomic.cost: Every thread of the target is suspended during the write burst (a few milliseconds in practice) — the target may appear to freeze for an instant. Limited to 32 addresses. Doesn't replace a simple write test beforehand to confirm these are actually the right addresses.
writeAtomic.example: A value shown on screen never changes despite individual writes that verify correctly in memory. A repeated next scan reveals 2 addresses that always stay equal to each other. Selecting both and clicking "Write together (atomic)" finally makes the write stick — the target was comparing the two copies and reverting the one that didn't match the other.

writeKernel.title: Write via kernel
writeKernel.what: Writes the value through the KillEngineKernel driver (KeStackAttachProcess on the driver side, not usermode WriteProcessMemory) instead of a normal write. This is an access-path escalation: it proves KillEngine can read/write from ring 0 when the driver is loaded.
writeKernel.when: Use it after a scan has been reduced to a small candidate set, especially when a normal write fails or when you want to verify that the kernel path works. Requires the KillEngineKernel driver to be loaded (Settings > Kernel driver > Test driver) — the button stays hidden otherwise. If the value still reverts after a successful kernel write, the important lesson is that the address is probably not the source of truth: run "Find what writes", then "Test automatically".
writeKernel.cost: Requires the kernel driver installed and loaded (see Settings). One address at a time, never bulk. Read the address before and after writing so the proof is clear.
writeKernel.example: Solitaire score: scan 175, next scan 185, two candidates. Kernel-read both addresses, kernel-write 1337 to the right one, kernel-read again, then confirm visually in the game. If one address reverts immediately, it is probably a copy or a recomputed value.

speedhack.title: Speedhack
speedhack.what: Injects a component into the attached process that hooks its time functions (QueryPerformanceCounter, GetTickCount, GetTickCount64, timeGetTime) and scales the returned value by a factor — speeds up or slows down anything based on them (animations, cooldowns, physics, timers).
speedhack.when: To speed through a wait (farming, load times) or slow down a hard section — same idea as Cheat Engine's speedhack. The factor can be adjusted live while active, no need to restart. The "Pause (0x)" preset fully freezes the clock the target perceives.
speedhack.cost: Code injection into the target process: same risk tier as "Write via kernel", confirmation required. Only covers modules already loaded at activation time, not calls resolved dynamically via GetProcAddress. Some protected software may detect or refuse the injection.
speedhack.example: A load time or repetitive farming grind takes too long. Enable speedhack at 4x from the Speedhack panel, or ask the Assistant to "speed up the game": animations and timers run 4x faster, disable to return to normal.

network.title: Network
network.intro: Analyze and control network traffic of the attached process.
network.what: Adds (or removes) a dedicated Windows Firewall rule blocking all inbound/outbound traffic for the attached process's executable.
network.when: To check whether an unstable memory value comes from a background server sync rather than a purely local reallocation — block the network, observe whether the behavior changes, then restore it once the test is done.
network.cost: Modifies the Windows Firewall via a UAC prompt (explicit elevation): same risk tier as speedhack, confirmation required. The rule persists even after detaching the process, until explicitly restored.
network.example: A displayed counter doesn't match any stable memory address despite several scans. Block the process's network, vary the counter in-game (offline), and see if the scan converges better — if so, the value likely depends on a server sync.

proxy.title: HTTP Proxy
proxy.intro: Intercepts and modifies HTTP/HTTPS requests from the game in real time.

dnsSpoof.title: DNS Spoof
dnsSpoof.intro: Redirects a domain to a local IP via the Windows hosts file.

lagSwitch.title: Lag switch
lagSwitch.intro: Artificially delays the game's network responses.

block.title: Network block
block.intro: Blocks all inbound/outbound traffic of the attached process via a Windows Firewall rule.

pointerChains.title: Pointer chains
pointerChains.what: Finds a stable module + offsets path to the address, instead of the absolute address that changes on every launch.
pointerChains.when: When an address stops working after the program restarts.
pointerChains.cost: Read only, but this is the slowest scan. Start with a depth of 3 before raising it.
pointerChains.example: Address 0x7FF6... worked yesterday but not today after relaunching the game. Run a pointer scan on it: you get a path like module+0x1A4 -> +0x20 -> +0x8, stable across sessions.

groupScan.title: Group scan
groupScan.what: Searches several known values separated by fixed offsets, for example HP at +0 and Mana at +4.
groupScan.when: When you know two or three neighbouring values: it locates the structure base in one pass.
groupScan.example: You know HP=100 and Mana=50 sit next to each other in memory. Enter both values with their relative offsets (0 and +4): KillEngine locates the player structure's base directly.

watchPointerChains.title: Watch pointer chains
watchPointerChains.what: Follows the value at the end of a pointer chain live, resolving it again on every tick.
watchPointerChains.when: To check a chain stays valid while the program reallocates its objects.
watchPointerChains.example: After validating a pointer chain, click Watch on it to confirm it keeps resolving to the right value even when the game recreates the object (level change, respawn...).

journal.title: Session journal
journal.what: Free-form note attached to the current analysis session.
journal.when: To record what worked before turning it into a profile or a Trainer feature.
journal.cost: No effect on the target process.
journal.example: Note "minerals AOB stable on patch 5.0.14" to remember later what worked, before turning it into a profile or a Trainer feature.

injection.title: Injection / hooking / auto-assembler
injection.what: Injects a DLL, installs an inline hook on a function, or runs an auto-assembler script inside the attached process.
injection.when: For an invincible freeze that intercepts the write at the source, or a cheat that needs to run inside the target process rather than read/write it from the outside.
injection.cost: Actively modifies the target process (injected code, rewritten instructions). Requires explicit confirmation for every action, no persistent Trainer feature yet.
injection.example: After capturing the instruction that writes a value (Written by), install a hook on it to force the value on every call instead of rewriting it in a loop from the outside.

inlineHook.title: Inline hook (address to address)
inlineHook.what: Redirects execution at a precise address to another memory address (your own already-injected code), via a trampoline that lets it return to the original code afterward. Unlike an AOB patch, the intercepted instruction is never rewritten in place — the redirect is cleanly removed with "Remove hook".
inlineHook.when: When you already know the exact address to intercept (found via "Written by" or "Disassemble backward") and want to branch to custom code instead of rewriting a value in a loop from the outside.
inlineHook.cost: Actively modifies the instructions at the target address and allocates a trampoline in memory. Requires knowing both the target address AND the address of already-injected hook code — not an automatic shortcut for a simple value (see "Force value (hook)" on a Written by capture for that specific case).
inlineHook.example: After capturing the instruction that writes health via Written by, enter its address as the target and the address of your already-injected hook function, then click Install hook — every call now runs through your code before resuming normally.

apiHook.title: Function interception (MinHook)
apiHook.what: Places a MinHook inline hook on a named function in a loaded module (e.g. kernel32.dll!Sleep) without knowing its address beforehand — KillEngine resolves it by name. Two modes: Count (the original function runs normally, only the call count is recorded) or Force return (the function never runs, a fixed return value is sent back instead).
apiHook.when: To confirm a function is really being called before patching it (Count mode), or to simulate a specific condition without touching the program's code (Force return mode, e.g. forcing an "access denied" return to test error handling).
apiHook.cost: Injects a component into the target process and changes its execution live. Force return mode only works for functions whose return value is a simple integer/pointer/bool — not more complex types (struct by value, etc.).
apiHook.example: Enter kernel32.dll and Sleep in Count mode, then click Intercept: every call to Sleep() in the program is now counted without changing its behavior — useful to confirm a suspected function is really causing a slowdown before going further.

clrGuide.title: CLR guided flow
clrGuide.what: Shows where you are in the CLR Inspector flow: process attached, CLR session active, objects listed, object selected to act on.
clrGuide.when: On first opening the CLR view, to see which step is still needed before you can read or write an object.
clrGuide.cost: Read only. The CLR heap can move after a garbage collection (GC): for a target that must survive that, prefer the field locator and a CLR Trainer feature over a remembered raw address.
clrGuide.example: Step 1 pending? Attach a .NET/CoreCLR process first via the Process view. Step 2 pending? Click Attach CLR to start the ClrMD helper.

clrAttach.title: Attach the CLR helper
clrAttach.what: Launches a dedicated .NET process (ClrMD) that attaches to the target's managed runtime to explore its heap, and lists objects whose type name contains the filter.
clrAttach.when: Only on a real .NET Framework/CoreCLR process (not Mono, not IL2CPP, not UWP .NET Native). The Objects button returns nothing if the filter is too narrow or empty on a large heap.
clrAttach.cost: Read only on attach. Roots lists known GC roots (stacks, statics). Flush GC cache forces ClrMD to re-read the current state after a GC or a large mutation on the target — useful if displayed objects look stale.
clrAttach.example: Filter `KillEngine.ClrTestTarget` then click Objects: the list only shows types from that namespace, easier to browse than the whole heap.

clrManualRead.title: Read a known address
clrManualRead.what: Directly describes the managed object at the address you paste in, without going through the list or a locator.
clrManualRead.when: When you already have a valid CLR object address, e.g. found via another view (GC root path, report, earlier read).
clrManualRead.cost: Read only. A remembered address becomes invalid after a compacting GC moves the object — prefer the stable Locator for a target that must survive a restart or a GC.
clrManualRead.example: Paste `0x2476e00acd8` then Enter: if the address still holds a live managed object, its fields appear in the Object read panel.

clrLocator.title: Stable locator (find by identity)
clrLocator.what: Searches the heap for every object of a given type whose identity field (e.g. Name) matches a value — instead of depending on a memory address that changes on every restart or compacting GC.
clrLocator.when: As soon as you want to reuse a target later (Trainer feature, profile, repeated write): a raw address doesn't survive a game restart, a locator does.
clrLocator.cost: Read only, scans the heap up to Max results. A poorly chosen identity field (a value that changes, like a score) will make relocation fail later — pick a stable field (name, unique id).
clrLocator.example: Type `KillEngine.ClrTestTarget.Player`, field `Name`, value `TestSubject` → Find. Click a result to read it, same as in the Objects table.

clrPathWrite.title: Symbolic path
clrPathWrite.what: Describes where a primitive field to write lives by name instead of by address — can traverse references (`Inventory.Items[0].Value`) and array/list indexes.
clrPathWrite.when: To write a field that isn't directly in the selected object's field table, or to build a reusable path independent of each sub-object's exact address.
clrPathWrite.cost: Only writes the final primitive field of the path (never a whole object or struct). Check "Use a locator" so the path is resolved from an object found by identity instead of the currently read address — survives a GC move in between.
clrPathWrite.example: Inventory object read, path `Items[0].Value`, value `999` → Write path only changes the Value field of the first item in the Items collection.

clrBatchWrite.title: Multi-field transaction
clrBatchWrite.what: Applies several symbolic-path writes in order, one per line (`Path=Value`), and tries to roll back the ones already applied if a later operation fails.
clrBatchWrite.when: To change several related fields together (e.g. a character's Health and Mana) without leaving the object in an inconsistent state if one write fails.
clrBatchWrite.cost: Best-effort: rollback restores the old value but doesn't guarantee perfect atomicity against the game reading concurrently. Checking "Suspend the process" adds a real suspension of every target thread during the write (safer, riskier if it deadlocks).
clrBatchWrite.example: `Health=100` and `Stats.Rank=7` on two lines then Transaction: both fields change together; if `Stats.Rank` fails, `Health` is restored to its original value.

clrCallSetter.title: Call a real setter
clrCallSetter.what: Resolves the already-JITted native address of the real C# setter via ClrMD, builds a small x64 shellcode (this in RCX, value in RDX/XMM1) and runs it by injection in the attached process — unlike the writes above (passive memory), this executes the real business logic (validation, side effects).
clrCallSetter.when: When writing the backing field directly isn't enough because the setter does more than assign the value (clamping, a separate counter, syncing another field).
clrCallSetter.cost: Code injection into the target process — a risky action, requires explicit confirmation. Instance setters only, 0 or 1 parameter, either primitive or a reference type (class/string, given as the hex address of an already-existing object — never a struct). The setter must already have run once in-game (JIT) or the call fails cleanly.
clrCallSetter.example: Property `Vitality`, value `999` → Call actually runs `set_Vitality(999)` in the target, with its clamp and change counter, not just a raw memory rewrite of the backing field.

clrDisassemble.title: Disassemble a setter (read-only)
clrDisassemble.what: Reuses the same ClrMD resolution as calling a setter to find a method's already-JITted native address, then disassembles the x64 code forward, instruction by instruction.
clrDisassemble.when: To understand what a setter actually does before calling it, or to find where to patch/hook once the location is known.
clrDisassemble.cost: Read only, never executes the target code. The method must already have been JITted (called at least once) or there's no native address yet to disassemble.
clrDisassemble.example: Method `set_Vitality`, 24 instructions → Disassemble shows the clamp and the backing-field write in x64 assembly, without ever executing anything.

clrReport.title: Generate an object report
clrReport.what: Exports the selected object and its reachable managed graph (fields, collections, optional GC root path) as a text document, walking references up to a bounded depth and node count.
clrReport.when: To save or share a complex object's state without re-navigating everything live in the other panels.
clrReport.cost: Read only. A large graph gets truncated (depth, node count, or time budget reached) — raise the bounds if the report looks incomplete, at the cost of a slower call.
clrReport.example: Inventory object selected, depth 3, 50 max nodes → Generate produces text listing the object, its fields, and the objects it references up to 3 hops away.

clrGcRootPath.title: Root → object path (exploratory)
clrGcRootPath.what: Reconstructs the shortest path from a GC root (stack, static...) to the target object through several reference hops — an approximate equivalent of `!gcroot` (SOS/WinDbg).
clrGcRootPath.when: To understand why an object stays alive (what references it), or to build a stable navigation path to it instead of remembering its address.
clrGcRootPath.cost: Read only. Bounded breadth-first search (depth/nodes/time on the helper side) — can be slow or find nothing on a very large heap.
clrGcRootPath.example: Selected object → Selected object (button) then Find path shows the full chain, e.g. `StrongHandle → Inventory → Items[2]` down to the target object.

clrFieldTable.title: Fields of the read object
clrFieldTable.what: Lists the selected object's fields with their type (Kind), effective memory address, and value. A `ref` value can be opened with Read; a writable field can be written directly, turned into a Trainer feature, or used as the identity field for a locator.
clrFieldTable.when: The simplest starting point to explore an object: no need to know a symbolic path for a field that's already visible here.
clrFieldTable.cost: Reading is safe. Writing a field here changes the backing memory directly (no setter execution, no business validation) — for that, use the "Call a setter" panel below.
clrFieldTable.example: Field `Health` with a Write button → type `100`, click Write: the memory value changes immediately, without going through the game's logic.

clrRootsTable.title: GC roots
clrRootsTable.what: Lists the roots ClrMD knows about — strong handles, stack variables, static fields — each pointing to a managed object that stays alive as long as its root exists.
clrRootsTable.when: To understand what's keeping an object alive, or as a starting point to rebuild a root → object path in the panel below.
clrRootsTable.cost: Read only. On a large heap the list can be long and may miss some StaticVar-kind roots (a known limitation of passive ClrMD attach, worked around elsewhere by a dedicated resolution).
clrRootsTable.example: A `StrongHandle` root pointing to the `Player` object explains why that object is never collected by the GC while the handle exists.
